title: UNHCR Bangladesh - Operational Update July August 2026
content:
KEY UPDATES

● NINTH ANNIVERSARY: To mark nine years of displacement, the Rohingya community in Cox’s Bazar held rallies in four camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf on 25 August. Over 100,000 people reportedly joined, calling for international attention to the crisis, sustained donor support and safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar when conditions allow. Media coverage focused on the protracted nature of the crisis, with more than 1.2 million refugees, and existing barriers to repatriation. 24 news reports by national and international outlets featured fulllength interviews, quotes or photo galleries facilitated by UNHCR, including two in-depth interviews with UNHCR Representative Ivo Freijsen (Al Jazeera and The Daily Star).

● NEW ARRIVALS: New arrivals continue to approach UNHCR in Cox’s Bazar camps to be biometrically identified, with 1,656 individuals newly identified in July and August, bringing the total to 155,296 individuals (40,838 families) biometrically identified since the exercise was launched in January 2025. Unlike regular refugee registration, suspended by the Government since May 2022, individual refugee identity documents are not issued through this process.
UNHCR continues to advocate with government counterparts for full registration and access to safe shelters for new arrivals.

● POST-REGISTRATION MONITORING: A Post-Registration Monitoring and Evaluation exercise — an independent assessment of refugees’ experience of registration services conducted in July by UNHCR and partner ACTED — found an overall 97% satisfaction rate. The 1,716 respondents included persons with specific needs and new arrivals. Areas for improvement include long waiting times, distance and access barriers, limited awareness of complaints and feedback channels, timely closure of cases and feedback on queries. The exercise will be conducted again in six months.

● STRATEGIC TRANSFORMATION OF THE ROHINGYA RESPONSE: UNHCR’s phase-out from Public Health programming continued, with five health facilities due to be handed over by endSeptember once UNHCR and the Health Sector jointly confirm best-fit partners. Two nutrition facilities on Bhasan Char island were transferred to UNICEF and WFP on 1 August, along with documentation, equipment and furniture, ensuring uninterrupted services for children and pregnant and breastfeeding women. The transition of all UNHCR distribution points to a new vendor for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) following the joint IOM/UNHCR tender also continued with no disruption to distribution.

● LANDSLIDES & DISASTER RISK REDUCTION: In July and August, 426 landslides were reported across the camps, causing 21 injuries and 15 deaths. UNHCR and partners coordinated rescue operations and worked with authorities on safety measures, including demolition of unsafe structures. Over the same period in 2025, 183 incidents were reported, causing two injuries and one death. The sharp rise in incidents, injuries and fatalities reflects overcrowding and funding cuts to disaster risk reduction activities, compounded by increased weather events and inadequate infrastructures. UNHCR continues monsoon preparedness and emergency response activities including volunteer mobilization, high-risk household relocation, community-led site improvement initiatives, drain cleaning, community awareness and emergency shelter support. UNHCR continues to advocate with authorities for additional land allocation to ease congestion in the camps.

title: UNICEF Guinea-Bissau Humanitarian Flash Update No. 3 (Mpox Outbreak Response), 14 August - 30 September 2026
content:
Highlights

  • Transmission remains a concern: As of 27 September, 23 confirmed cases and 135 suspected cases had been reported across SAB, Biombo and Bafatá, with no deaths. The source of infection is unknown for 74% of confirmed cases, highlighting gaps in surveillance and contact tracing.
  • Protecting young children is a priority: Three confirmed cases are infants aged approximately 11–12 months, underscoring the need for close clinical follow-up, household investigations and prevention measures as schools reopen.
  • UNICEF is expanding prevention support: including WASH supplies and information materials for 50 health facilities, alongside posters and comic books for more than 5,000 public-school classrooms in the three affected regions.
  • Flexible funding is urgently needed: UNICEF requires approximately US$250,000 for priority interventions and will adapt its response as the Ministry plans to extend the national response plan by a further six months.

title: Mauritania | Population Movement Operation Update #4 (MDRMR017)
content:
A. SITUATION ANALYSIS

Description of the crisis

Humanitarian Situation and Needs Overview

Deteriorating Security Situation in Mali

Continued insecurity and violence in central and northern Mali are contributing to population movements into Mauritania. Disruption of livelihoods, reduced access to basic services and persistent protection concerns continue to affect communities in Mali and contribute to displacement towards neighbouring areas of Mauritania.

Hodh Chargui, in south-eastern Mauritania, continues to receive a significant proportion of people arriving from Mali. As of 31 August 2026, UNHCR estimated that Mauritania was hosting approximately 305,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, of whom 189,881 were registered nationally. Of these, 177,542 registered refugees were in Hodh Chargui.

Cross-Border Implications and Population Movements

Continued population movements from Mali are placing additional pressure on communities and services in Hodh Chargui. Refugees and returnees arriving in border areas require access to shelter, safe water, sanitation, health care, protection and other essential services.

A significant proportion of refugees are living within host communities rather than in Mbera Camp. Earlier in 2026, UNHCR reported that more than 170,000 refugees were living across over 70 host villages in Hodh Chargui, in addition to approximately 120,000 people in Mbera Camp.2 This settlement pattern places additional pressure on local infrastructure, services and natural resources, while increasing the importance of assistance that addresses the needs of both displaced and host populations.

Protection concerns remain significant, particularly for women, children and people with specific vulnerabilities. Displacement and repeated exposure to insecurity can also increase psychosocial distress, family separation and protection risks, reinforcing the need for accessible referral mechanisms and community-based protection and psychosocial support.

Conditions and Unmet Humanitarian Needs

Refugees, returnees and vulnerable host communities continue to face gaps in access to adequate shelter, safe water, sanitation, food, health care, protection and livelihood opportunities. These challenges are particularly pronounced in remote communities where access to services and humanitarian assistance remains limited.

Pressure on water, pasture and other natural resources also affects host communities whose existing coping capacities are already constrained. Continued arrivals therefore increase demand for basic services and may contribute to tensions over access to limited resources.

Public health risks remain a concern, particularly where communities have limited access to safe water and adequate sanitation. Continued community-based health promotion, disease surveillance, referrals and early identification of malnutrition remain important components of the response.

Compounding Risks: Climate and Environmental Hazards

The humanitarian situation is further compounded by recurrent climate-related shocks, including flooding, drought, bushfires and environmental degradation. These hazards affect livelihoods, water availability, pasture, infrastructure and humanitarian access, particularly in remote areas.

The combined effects of displacement, limited access to essential services and climate-related shocks continue to increase the vulnerability of both displaced and host communities and place additional pressure on existing coping mechanisms.

Operational Capacity and Humanitarian Response

The Mauritanian Red Crescent (MRC), with support from the IFRC, continues to provide humanitarian assistance across Bassikounou, Néma, Amourj and Adel Bagrou, focusing on refugees, returnees and vulnerable host communities.

The response includes shelter, multipurpose cash assistance, water, sanitation and hygiene, health, protection, migration, and community engagement and accountability activities. Two Humanitarian Service Points in Dowinkara and Fassala continue to support people on the move through first aid, psychological first aid, information, referrals and other essential services.

Implementation has, however, been affected by funding constraints, competing operational demands, the remoteness of the intervention areas and supply-chain capacity gaps. These challenges have affected procurement follow-up, supplier settlement and the timely completion of some planned activities.

To strengthen supply-chain capacity and facilitate completion of the remaining activities, the IFRC has recruited a full-time Supply Chain Delegate to support procurement follow-up, verification of supplier deliveries, stock reconciliation, transport arrangements and completion of outstanding procurement processes.

The MRC and IFRC will continue coordinating with local authorities and humanitarian partners to complete the remaining activities within the existing operational scope, while maintaining a strong focus on protection, accountability and the priority needs of affected communities.

title: Ukraine war situation update | 19 – 25 September 2026
content:
Ukraine’s strikes knock out refining capacity at a Moscow refinery, while Russia targets Ukrainian communications.

Author Tetiana Gaviuk

Key trends

  • Ukraine’s forces struck the Kapotnya oil refinery, a critical supplier of fuel to Moscow, as well as refineries in the Republic of Bashkortostan and the Samara, Rostov, and Krasnodar regions, along with oil storage and transport infrastructure, further reducing Russian oil production and processing capabilities. While the Kapotnya oil refinery was previously struck in June, the scale of the most recent strike, which resulted in an operational shutdown of the refinery’s crude-oil processing capacity, points to escalatory action in response to recent pushes for an energy ceasefire. Against the backdrop of renewed discussion about potential peace talks, possibly hosted by the UAE, Ukraine should be expected to maintain or intensify its campaign against Russian oil and energy infrastructure until any such negotiations take place.
  • Russia launched an intense multi-day barrage against Kyiv, leaving at least 59 civilians injured and causing extensive damage to civilian infrastructure and residential buildings across the city and the surrounding region. Several strikes appear to have deliberately targeted internet and communication infrastructure in the capital, including the first recorded strike on a major data center in the capital. While Ukraine’s decentralized communication network could prevent a prolonged countrywide internet shutdown, Russia's continuous attacks on data-processing centers and data storage facilities have the potential to cause disruption at the local and regional levels, likely affecting internet access, services, and business operations.

Key events

20 Sep.

Moscow, Russia – A Ukrainian large-scale combined drone and missile attack against the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya forces the suspension of operations

22 Sep.

Slovyansk — A Russian FPV drone strikes an aid warehouse, killing a volunteer and destroying a water delivery truck

24 Sep.

Kyiv – Russian drones and missiles strike a major data center and a telecom data processing facility in the city of Kyiv over two days

title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #7 (October 6, 2026)
content:
FAST FACTS

  • As of October 5, 459 cholera cases and four deaths had been reported in Minawao Refugee Camp, which currently is home to more than 81,000 refugees and operating at about 325% of intended capacity.
  • Multiple transmission chains are suspected within the camp, where heavy rainfall is increasing the risk of rapid spread among vulnerable populations.
  • Nationwide, according to the most recent government figures, there have been 2,903 confirmed cases and 84 deaths nationwide across 13 health districts.
  • The cholera outbreak in Cameroon has a case fatality rate of 2.89%, which is nearly three times higher than the internationally accepted target of less than 1%.

OUR RESPONSE

  • International Medical Corps has been operating in Minawao Refugee Camp since 2013, providing Nigerian refugees with primary, community-based and referred secondary healthcare.
  • In response to the outbreak, our team has treated all 459 patients, expanded the cholera treatment unit to 65 beds, trained 105 health workers in case management and infection prevention, and reached a daily average of 6,478 people through community information sessions on hygiene, safe water and early care-seeking.
  • We are coordinating with national health authorities, United Nations agencies, camp management and humanitarian partners to support a coordinated response.

title: Global Weather Hazards Summary, October 08, 2026 – October 14, 2026
content:
Global Overview: El Niño continues to strengthen. Although long-term abnormal dryness persists in several regions, heavy rain is causing flooding in parts of central and northern Africa, eastern Central Asia, Central America, and northern South America.

Africa Weather Hazards

Abnormal heat is forecast in the eastern Sahel and parts of Eastern Africa, while high risks of flooding exist in far-western West Africa, Morocco, and southern Ethiopia.

1) Inundation in the Sudd wetlands of South Sudan persists.
2) Large 90-day rainfall deficits have led to abnormal dryness across Chad and large parts of Eastern Africa. As a result, deteriorated vegetation conditions, driven by drought, have been observed over western Sudan, southern and southeastern South Sudan, northern Uganda, and parts of Ethiopia's northern, eastern, and central regions.
3) Central Mali and central/eastern Liberia and southern Cote D’Ivoire are under Abnormal Dryness because of sustained below-average rainfall over the past 30 and 90 days.
4) Recent heavy rainfall has caused flooding in Anambra and Delta States in Nigeria.
5) The forecast heavy rainfall elevates flood risk in western Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea-Conakry, Sierra Leone, Liberia, northern Morocco, southern Ethiopia, and parts of Somalia during the next week.
6) Abnormal heat is forecast in southern Chad, eastern CAR, Sudan, South Sudan, northern Uganda, and northwestern Kenya as above-average temperatures are expected to persist for three or more consecutive days in this region during the next week.

title: Syrian Arab Republic - Emergency Mobility Tracking and Cross Border Monitoring Situation Update - Round 23 (05 October 2026)
content:
OVERVIEW

Cross-border movements from Lebanon into Syria have remained broadly stable in recent months, with the gradual pattern observed following the 17 April 2026 ceasefire continuing through the reporting period. From 2 March to 5 October, DTM recorded 130,598 arrivals across 1,187 communities in all 14 governorates. Syrian nationals continued to account for the overwhelming majority of arrivals, while Lebanese nationals represented less than 1 per cent.

Flow monitoring at four assessed Syrian-Lebanese border crossings recorded approximately 864,238 movements into Syria during the same period, comprising 98 per cent Syrian and 2 per cent Lebanese nationals. In addition, 4,480 Lebanese nationals were recorded transiting through Syria towards Jordan, reflecting the continued use of Syria as both a destination and transit route within wider regional movements.

Access conditions continued to shape movement across the different Points of Entry (PoEs). While Arida remained closed following its 6 August temporary closure for technical works on the Lebanese side, movements continued through the other assessed crossings. During the reporting period, Key Informants (KIs) reported needs related to transportation, basic assistance, and access to services at and beyond the crossings.

DTM continues to monitor cross-border movements and changes in access conditions, with current findings indicating that movement patterns have remained relatively gradual and stable.

title: Protection and Solutions Monitoring Flash Alert #22 - Lower Shabelle clashes displace over 5000 people to Afgooye
content:
Background

Between 29 August and 13 September 2026, security operations and related armed confrontations involving the Somali National Army (SNA) and non-state armed actors occurred in parts of Lower Shabelle Region, including Basra, Alifow, Baqdaad, Areer Mooge, and surrounding areas. The deterioration in the security environment during the reporting period contributed to the displacement of civilians and increased humanitarian needs among affected communities. The deteriorating security situation prompted affected communities to flee their homes, abandon livelihoods and productive assets in search of safety. The resulting displacement has disrupted access to essential services and increased the humanitarian and protection needs of displaced and affected households.

More than 860 households, approximately 5,100 individuals, were displaced from Basra, Baqdaad, Alifow, Beytalkariim, Areer Mooge, Jambalul and Walamooy to Afgooye town. The displaced population comprises 573 men, 947 women, and 3,640 children. Four children (two boys and two girls) and one older man were injured by gunfire. The man was transferred to Medina Hospital in Mogadishu, where he later died from his injuries.

Most displaced households have sought refuge in IDP settlements and surrounding communities in Afgooye, particularly in Carbiska, Lafoole and Xawo Abdi. The security situation in the areas of origin remains volatile, affecting civilian movement and limiting the possibility of an immediate return. Displaced families continue to face limited access to shelter, food, water, healthcare, and other essential services. In addition, approximately 620 children are currently out of school, increasing the risk of prolonged disruption to their education and heightened protection concerns.

PSMN identified 22 persons with disabilities (7 women and 15 men) among the displaced population. Most reportedly have physical or mental impairments and may face additional barriers in accessing information, humanitarian assistance and essential services. Their specific needs should be addressed through inclusive assistance, appropriate accommodation and referrals to relevant services, where available.

title: Emergency Protection Monitoring Report - July 2026
content:
During July 2026, the protection environment across monitored collective shelters in South Lebanon and the Bekaa remained characterized by protracted displacement, shelter consolidation measures, barriers to safe and dignified return, deteriorating socioeconomic conditions, and persistent gaps in access to essential services. While displacement trends differed between the two regions, monitoring findings indicate that the households remaining displaced increasingly represent some of the most vulnerable caseloads, facing complex and overlapping protection risks linked to insecurity, housing destruction, loss of livelihoods, financial hardship, and inadequate living conditions.

In South Lebanon, shelter closures emerged as major protection concerns throughout the reporting period. The closure of Lebanese University Faculty of Arts and continued shelter consolidation measures generated significant anxiety among displaced households, many of whom reported having limited accommodation alternatives. Families expressed concerns regarding overcrowding in receiving shelters, unaffordable rental costs, damaged homes in areas of origin, and the risk of repeated displacement.

In the Bekaa, the majority of displaced households had already returned following the ceasefire, leaving only a residual caseload residing in the remaining active collective shelters.

However, monitoring findings indicate that the remaining households in both areas face substantial barriers to return, including insecurity, extensive destruction of housing, loss of livelihoods, and the inability to secure alternative accommodation. These households continue to experience heightened protection risks associated with poverty, inadequate shelter and WASH services, healthcare barriers, and increasing reliance on negative coping mechanisms.

Across both operational areas, protection concerns extended beyond immediate displacement-related needs. Households consistently reported challenges accessing healthcare, food, safe water, and other essential services. Psychosocial distress remained widespread, while accountability concerns, unequal perceptions of assistance distribution, community tensions, and gaps affecting women, children, persons with disabilities, older persons, and female-headed households continued to undermine safety, dignity, well-being, and social cohesion.

Overall, findings indicate that despite localized improvements and humanitarian interventions, the remaining displaced population continues to face interconnected protection risks requiring sustained protection monitoring, accountability mechanisms, referrals, advocacy, and coordinated multi-sectoral support.

title: occupied Palestinian territory (oPt) Situation Analysis (7/9/2026 - 13/9/2026)
content:
Executive Summary

The Occupied Palestinian Territories face a catastrophic humanitarian crisis marked by severe food insecurity, mass displacement, and the near-collapse of essential services. In Gaza, the majority of the population relies entirely on humanitarian assistance, with widespread destruction of housing, health facilities, water infrastructure, and educational institutions compounding the challenges faced by displaced families. Harsh winter conditions, repeated evacuation orders, and constrained humanitarian access continue to threaten the safety and well-being of civilians, with children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups bearing a disproportionate burden.

In the West Bank, escalating military operations, settler violence, and movement restrictions have driven significant displacement and disrupted access to livelihoods, healthcare, and education. Economic contraction and rising unemployment have eroded household resilience, while demolitions and settlement expansion threaten further territorial fragmentation. Across both territories, humanitarian organizations are working to scale up food assistance, shelter support, health services, and protection programming, yet persistent access barriers, funding shortfalls, and ongoing hostilities continue to outpace the response, leaving Palestinians in urgent need of sustained international support and durable solutions.

title: WFP Senegal Country Brief, September 2026
content:
SITUATION OVERVIEW

• During the 2026 lean season, crisis or emergency food insecurity rose by 71 percent (compared to March – May 2026) to 836,786 people, highlighting weak household resilience.
Rising agricultural input costs and El Niñorelated impacts are expected to further worsen food insecurity in the 2027 lean season.
According to the latest Fill the Nutrient Gap assessment, 60 percent of the population lacks access to a healthy diet, while 46 percent cannot afford a nutritious diet.

• Against this backdrop, the Government of Senegal is advancing Sénégal 2050: Agenda National de Transformation (Jubbanti), which provides the national framework for human capital development, food sovereignty, youth employment, and climate resilience.

• WFP aligns its interventions with these priorities through its Country Strategic Plan (CSP) 2025– 2029, built on four pillars: (i) crisis response through food and nutrition assistance; (ii) prevention and treatment of malnutrition and school meals to support human capital; (iii) climate-smart livelihoods and sustainable food systems with a focus on women and youth; and (iv) strengthening national systems through technical assistance and capacity development.

title: Attacks on Health Care in Sudan, 16 - 30 September 2026
content:
Data by Insecurity Insight shows that since fighting started between the SAF and RSF in April 2023 and 30 September 2026 at least 794 incidents of violence against or obstruction of access to health care took place across Sudan:

  • health facilities were damaged 224 times
  • 221 health workers were killed, 16 kidnapped and 142 arrested

Drone strikes damaging health facilities surged by 88% in the first eight months of 2026, rising from 16 such cases in 2025 to 30 between January and September 2026. Two-thirds of these incidents were attributed to the RSF, with health facilities in Kordofan particularly affected. SAF drone strikes also increasingly damaged health facilities between January and April, mostly in Darfur and Kordofan.

title: Yemen Protection Overview Brief - 03 Oct 2026
content:
Yemen: Escalating Protection Risks
Displacement, access constraints and mounting pressure on internally displaced people, refugees and host communities

Situation at a glance

The latest military escalation in Yemen has displaced growing numbers of people at an alarming rate, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis and intensifying existing protection concerns. Families uprooted from the West Coast, Taiz, Lahj and Marib are fleeing their homes carrying limited belongings while facing insecurity, high transportation costs, and shortages of food, water and medicines. Host communities continue to provide support; however, reduced assistance, increasing pressure on already overstretched services, and competition over limited resources risk weakening social cohesion. Many of the newly displaced families have already experienced multiple waves of displacement, further exhausting their coping capacities, depleting their resources, and increasing their exposure to protection risks. As the conflict and insecurity intensify, displacement patterns are expanding beyond traditional hotspots, with growing movements from Taiz towards Lahj, Aden and Abyan, placing additional pressure on host communities, public services and humanitarian response capacities.

title: Desert Locust Bulletin 576 (6 October 2026)
content:
ISOLATED ADULTS IN THE WESTERN REGION

In September, the general locust situation appeared calm across the three desert locust breeding Regions. In the Western Region, solitarious adult populations continued to be present in Mauritania and Chad, but no locusts were seen in Algeria and Tunisia. No surveys were conducted in Mali and Niger. In the Central Region, isolated adults were seen in Egypt, and no locusts were seen in Sudan, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Oman. In the Eastern Region, no locusts were seen in Iran, Pakistan and India. During the forecast period, summer breeding in Mauritania, southern Algeria, northern Mali and Niger, and Chad could result in increasing locust populations in the Western Region, where hopper and adult groups may form by the end of the forecast period. Surveys should continue in the summer breeding areas of these countries as the ecological conditions are favorable for breeding, and preventive control may be required. In the Central Region, small-scale breeding may occur in the summer areas of Sudan, the western lowlands of Eritrea and the interior areas of Yemen. Small-scale winter breeding may begin on the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden coastal plains, but no significant developments are expected. In the Eastern Region, summer breeding may occur along the Indo-Pakistan border; however, no significant developments are expected.

title: Yemen Situation: UNHCR Emergency Update - External Update #3 (05 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

▪ In Yemen, UNHCR is part of the inter-agency response under the Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). In light of the recent escalation, UNHCR requires US$ 25 million to support an estimated 231,000 people with protection services, including monitoring, legal assistance and support for people at heightened risk, cash assistance, shelter and core relief items (CRIs). A 115 tonne shipment of essential relief items is en route to Yemen to help meet the immediate needs of around 30,000 people affected by the recent escalation.

▪ More than 174,000 people have been newly displaced inside Yemen since 1 August, while 3,986 people have arrived in Eastern Africa, including 3,799 refugees in Obock, Djibouti, and 187 Somali refugees who voluntarily returned from Yemen to Somalia through UNHCR’s Assisted Spontaneous Return programme. Women and children account for 75% of new arrivals. The average family size is 3.8 persons, down from six among displaced families in Yemen, indicating that many individuals have been forced to leave family members behind.

title: Eastern Chad - Sudanese Situation - Flash Updates #58 (28 September 2026)
content:
UPDATE ON SITUATION IN SUDAN

Context

The security situation along Chad-Sudan borders remains a concern, although condition within the country is generally stable. The border provinces of Wadi Fira, Ennedi Est, and Ouaddaï continue to be affected by the spillover effects of the conflict in neighbouring Sudan. The ongoing crisis continues to drive people to seek safety in Chad while also impacting border communities and humanitarian operations.

Recent reports indicate continued insecurity and armed clashes in several parts of Sudan, including North Kordofan, North Darfur, and South Darfur. As hostilities persist and frontlines shift, civilian populations continue to face significant protection risks and new waves of displacement. In Nyala, South Darfur, residents reported renewed aerial strikes on 27 September following a period of relative calm.

The continued conflict exposes civilian populations to heightened protection risks, including injuries and loss of life caused by hostilities, forced displacement, disruption of livelihoods, and reduced access to essential services. Humanitarian actors remain concerned about the impact of the intensification of military operations on civilians, particularly in areas regularly affected by conflict and insecurity.

In addition to conflict-related challenges, several regions of Sudan are experiencing worsening climatic conditions. Below-average rainfall, degraded grazing land, and increasing water scarcity are undermining livelihoods, particularly for communities dependent on agriculture and livestock. The combined effects of conflict, drought, and declining access to natural resources are increasingly driving population movements towards safer areas, including eastern Chad. New arrivals interviewed at the border frequently cited insecurity, along with its consequences, including the loss of livelihoods, as key factors that prompted their departure. Insufficient rainfall and the drying up of water sources have further exacerbated the erosion of livelihoods, making already precarious living conditions even more difficult.

title: UNHCR Egypt - Factsheet - September 2026
content:
Some 1,084,858 refugees and asylum-seekers are registered with UNHCR Egypt. Sudanese are the largest group—over ¾— followed by Syrians. Most live in Greater Cairo and Alexandria.

Egypt is the top recipient country of people fleeing the current conflict in Sudan. UNHCR is intensifying its protection and assistance efforts to meet the most urgent needs of newly arrived Sudanese refugees.

Egypt enacted its first asylum law in December 2024 and issued its by-laws in May 2026, establishing a national framework for refugee management and protection. UNHCR supports the government in its implementation.

title: Mozambique Conflict Monitor Update: October 2026
content:
Overview

Over August and September, Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) has increasingly targeted civilians in Mocimboa da Praia, Muidumbe, and Macomia districts. In September, the group returned to threaten communities in Nangade. The response in Mocímboa da Praia town has been to tighten security measures, which has constrained commercial and humanitarian activity. As a result, the town is likely to become more tense. That tension may be directed toward the state, either through protests or increased collaboration with ISM.

Evidence suggests that ISM’s return to Nangade is to draw on support from neighboring Tanzania, a development likely to lead to tightened security measures on both sides of the border.

Meanwhile, the early October release of hostages taken by ISM in Niassa province last month in return for ransom is likely to embolden the group to target foreigners for abduction in the future. This will concern humanitarian organizations across Cabo Delgado, mining companies active around the Montepuez district, and Niassa province’s tourism sector.

ISM releases hostages in a Montepuez standoff

On 4 October, three hostages whom ISM had abducted during the 3 September raid on a hunting camp in Niassa were released. This was in return for a ransom of 3.2 million meticais (roughly $53,000 at the time), according to a local source. The three, a South African, a Zimbabwean, and a Mozambican, had been held since early September in the Shamba Kubwa mining area of Nairoto in the north of Montepuez district.

The release followed a standoff of over three weeks between ISM in the Shamba Kubwa area and the Defense Armed Forces of Mozambique (FADM) based in Ntola village, approximately 45 kilometers south.

FADM did not attempt an assault on Shamba Kubwa, likely due to the presence of hostages. ISM may have also deployed IEDs on approach to Shamba Kubwa from Ntola, according to a local source.

The group’s continued presence in the area suggests that they have a means of resupplying arms and ammunition. The group has likely developed a support network to facilitate this in Nairoto, having visited the area six months last year, and now three months in 2026. A local source also reports that the group has engaged in extortion at the mining site and also seized forestry equipment.

Their ability to resupply suggests that the group may consider staying in the area, rather than dispersing and returning to Macomia via the Meluco district, as past behavior suggests. This would stretch FADM’s capacity and present a continuing threat to civilians in Niassa, and tourism in particular.

Their ability to extract a significant ransom will likely encourage ISM in targeting high-value kidnap victims in the future, likely foreigners associated with businesses that have an international profile.

ISM’s increased civilian targeting supports multiple objectives

In September, ISM continued a trend of increasingly targeting civilians in Macomia, Mocímboa da Praia, Muidumbe, and Nangade districts, carrying out 19 attacks on civilians, up from 11 in August and nine in July. ISM targets civilians for three main purposes: to foment civilian displacement, generate income, and engage in retribution.

First, displacement can overwhelm civic and military authorities. Over August and September, attacks in Litandacua on the N380, and at Pangane on the coast, prompted over 700 people to flee, according to the International Organization for Migration. This creates opportunities for freedom of movement. September’s attacks on rural communities in Nangade are likely to have provided cover for ISM to maintain a connection to support networks in Tanzania for recruits and supplies. On 20 September, Tanzanian troops stationed in Nangade killed two suspected insurgents who had crossed from Tanzania, and arrested a third. A group of ISM fighters was later seen making its way to the Namatil area of Nangade, likely to receive the group intercepted by the Tanzanian military or others.

Second, income can be generated from ransom. Eleven attacks on civilian communities involved abductions, and ransoms were reported in five incidents, ranging from 1,500 to 70,000 meticais.

The third reason is retribution. ISM carried out at least three attacks in September on civilians on Macomia’s coast, an area in which ISM has established an area of influence, and in which attacks on civilians are rare. These act as a warning to communities suspected of collaborating with FADM and the Rwanda Defence Force, which have been conducting sporadic operations against ISM in Quiterajo, about 35 km to the north, including marine operations.

In the coming weeks, there is a risk that such actions will escalate in Cabo Delgado’s southern districts. In late September, ISM fighters in Quissanga were seen moving south toward the Ancuabe district. As in districts to the north, the group will pose a significant threat to isolated rural communities and artisanal and small-scale mining sites, and less so to commercial gemstone mining projects.

Security tightened in Mocímboa da Praia town

In September, ISM carried out attacks to the south, north, and west of Mocímboa da Praia town (see map below), in ways that continue to restrict humanitarian and commercial access to the town and allow ISM to maintain supply networks there. These attacks come as heightened security measures in September have raised tensions in the town, according to local sources.

With the airport closed and the N380 at risk, humanitarian access to the town is via Palma to the north. However, ISM attacks on the R762 illustrate the heightened risk faced on that route. Attacks to the west, likely carried out by a group operating from the Nkonga area of neighboring Nangade district, maintain pressure on the N380 and force rural communities back to Mocímboa da Praia town.

To the south, Islamic State media claimed that ISM successfully deployed an IED against an RDF patrol on the road linking Chinda village on the N380 to an RDF base at Mbau village, 30 km southwest of Mocímboa da Praia town, on 16 September. The combination of a poor road running through heavily forested land makes the road susceptible to such attacks, hindering state forces’ movement and allowing ISM to maintain its presence in the area.

Authorities in the town are concerned that ISM’s nearby presence allows suppliers operating in the town to easily reach ISM forces to supply them with cash, food, and other necessities. Authorities have responded to ISM activities in the area by restricting access from the town to surrounding areas and establishing checkpoints to prevent movement in or out of the town after 15:00, according to a source in the town. Within the town, there is a heightened security presence. FADM permanently guards the Administrator’s office, and the State Security and Intelligence Service has increased its presence, according to a local source. If the situation persists, straitened humanitarian services and commercial activity will lead to worsening conditions in the town, risking community unrest.

title: RB ESA Region: Regional Community Feedback Analysis Report (April – June 2026)
content:
Executive Summary

The second quarter of 2026 marked a significant milestone for the Regional Bureau for Eastern and Southern Africa (RB-ESA), with the first integration of Southern Africa operations into the regional community feedback reporting framework. Ten (10) country operations shared a total of 49,751 feedback entries, representing a 9% increase from 45,494 in Q1.

Requests for assistance and services accounted for more than half of all feedback (55%), up from 49% in Q1, while requests for information consisted of 41%, reflecting sustained humanitarian needs and demand for reliable information. Toll-free hotlines were the primary feedback channel used by most refugees (64.9%) and other forcibly displaced persons across the region.

The regional feedback resolution rate slightly declined from 68% to 62%. This was driven in part by a growing backlog of follow-up queries on previously reported cases due to reduced operational capacity to respond. This trend highlights increasing pressure on existing response systems and makes timely case management by operations even more important.

There is a need for operations to invest more in the capacity to respond to feedback, case management, and follow-up functions. This will help clear backlogs, improve resolution rates, and ensure that community feedback continues to shape protection and programme decision-making while sustaining trust and accountability to refugees and other forcibly displaced persons.

title: WFP Chad Country Brief, September 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

• A joint mission to Bol and Bagasola in Lac Province found that displacement, drought, and limited access to productive land continue to drive acute humanitarian needs, underscoring the need for strengthened food assistance and expanded resilience-building activities to support both displaced and host communities.

• Conducted jointly by WFP and UNHCR in coordination with the National Commission for Refugees and Returnees (CNARR), the vulnerabilitybased targeting assessment was completed and preparations for the transition to vulnerabilitybased assistance are underway, with rollout now expected in October 2026.

• Under the anticipatory action framework, 29,568 people received cash-based assistance in Lac Province.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

• From 10 to 15 August, the Food Security Cluster, the Cash Working Group, and the Ministry of Social Action, Solidarity and Humanitarian Affairs conducted a joint mission to Bol and Bagasola in Lac Province to assess humanitarian needs, response gaps, and market conditions for newly displaced people. The mission confirmed that the humanitarian situation remains critical, with continued population displacement and a high dependence on humanitarian assistance among both displaced and host communities. Stakeholders highlighted the increasing pressure on host households, which are simultaneously coping with the effects of drought and declining incomes. The mission also found that belowaverage rainfall is threatening agricultural production, the main livelihood source for many households, while limited access to productive land remains a major constraint for displaced populations.

title: Ukraine Situation - Moldova Operational Update (August 2026)
content:
OPERATIONAL CONTEXT

As of July 2026, 144,204 refugees from Ukraine are present in the Republic of Moldova. The latest Participatory Assessment indicates that refugees continue to view Moldova as a place of safety, stability and dignity, with many reporting a strong sense of belonging and positive relations with host communities.

As the response gradually shifts from humanitarian assistance towards inclusion in national systems, refugees highlighted increasing concerns regarding employment opportunities, housing affordability, healthcare, access to information, and uncertainty about their future legal status beyond the current Temporary Protection regime. Rising living costs, increasing rental and utility expenses, the ongoing consolidation of Refugee Accommodation Centres, limited livelihood opportunities, particularly in rural areas, and the reduction of humanitarian assistance are placing additional pressure on vulnerable households. Older people, persons with disabilities and refugees with specific needs remain at risk due to limited livelihood opportunities, health-related needs, barriers to specialized healthcare and social services. These trends highlight the importance of sustaining targeted support while advancing refugee inclusion in national systems, ensuring that vulnerable refugees are not left behind during the transition from emergency response to longer-term solutions.

title: Islamic Republic of Iran: Humanitarian Update No. 08 | As of 31 August 2026
content:
This Humanitarian Update is produced by OCHA Regional Office for the Middle East and North Africa (ROMENA) on behalf of and in collaboration with UN agencies and humanitarian organisations. It covers the period from 1 to 31 August 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • In southern and south-eastern areas, an estimated 200,000 people require humanitarian assistance following the re-escalation of hostilities in July. Up to 60 per cent of the fishing fleet reportedly remains inactive, disrupting the livelihoods of approximately 37,000 fishers. Damage to infrastructure and the presence of debris, coupled with forecast of above-average rainfall and potential flooding, continue to pose significant public health risks.
  • UN agencies are providing test kits for water-borne diseases and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) emergency supplies to support the restoration of safe drinking water. They are also assessing livelihood support needs in the fisheries sector.
  • An oil spill in August reportedly affected approximately 32,000 m² of Qeshm’s coastline and 90,000 m² of surrounding waters, raising concerns about its impact on marine and coastal ecosystems.

KEY FIGURES

3.4K+ Civilians killed (figure is for the period 28 February-14 September, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #11)

33K+ Civilians injured (figure is for the period 28 February-14 September, as reported by WHO Middle East Conflict Situation Report #11)

149K+ Civilian units damaged (figure is for the period since 28 February as reported by the Iranian Red Crescent Society on 7 June 2026)

SITUATION OVERVIEW

The humanitarian situation in Iran continues to be shaped by recurring escalations and their economic and operational consequences. Disruptions to basic services and infrastructure persist, while inflation and market uncertainty continue to erode household purchasing power. Restrictions on maritime and air transport routes, along with trade disruptions, have also affected the import and distribution of pharmaceutical supplies.

The July escalation increased humanitarian needs, particularly in the south. According to a local partner reporting to IOM, around 300,000 people were affected across Hormozgan, Bushehr, Khuzestan and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces, including an estimated 200,000 people in need of humanitarian assistance. Damage to water and electricity infrastructure has disrupted access to safe drinking water, while forecasts of above-average rainfall and potential flooding could further worsen humanitarian and public health risks.

An oil spill reported between 10 and 13 August from vessels damaged in the Strait of Hormuz affected an estimated 32,000 m² of coastline and 90,000 m² of surrounding waters off Qeshm Island, raising concerns over impacts on marine and coastal ecosystems. Cleanup operations were reported to be largely completed by 24 August.

HUMANITARIAN IMPACT AND NEEDS

Health

In southern and south-eastern areas, infrastructure damage and debris from the July escalation, combined with forecast of above-average rainfall and potential flooding linked to El Niño conditions, may increase the risk of dengue, malaria and other vector-borne diseases. Nationwide, out-of-pocket payments account for an estimated 43 per cent of total health expenditure, placing additional strain on households amid declining purchasing power. Continued support is needed to sustain essential health services, including cold chains, lifesaving medicines, diagnostic capacity, primary healthcare, and maternal and reproductive health services.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)

In August, the National Water and Wastewater Engineering Company reported that 410 water and wastewater networks and 2,000 electricity network assets had been damaged since March 2026, affecting power generation and water services. In Hormozgan, Isfahan and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces, damage caused by the July escalation has disrupted access to safe drinking water. Priority needs include repairing damaged infrastructure and restoring reliable water services for vulnerable populations in affected areas.

Food Security

Despite well-functioning markets, purchasing power continues to decline. Food inflation reached 128.1 per cent in July 2026, compared with headline year-on-year inflation of 87.9 per cent. Although the minimum wage increased by 60 per cent in March-April 2026, real food purchasing power remained around 30 per cent lower than a year earlier, while the gap between income and minimum expenditure widened by 137 per cent. Food assistance needs remain significant among conflict-affected households, particularly those reliant on fisheries and coastal livelihoods in Hormozgan, Sistan and Baluchestan, and Bushehr provinces.

Protection

The reported disruptions to health services, water and sanitation systems, and livelihoods disproportionately affect children under five, pregnant and lactating women, women-headed households, persons with disabilities, Afghan refugees, and other vulnerable groups. Access to mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), protection services, and essential dignity and menstrual hygiene supplies remains a priority, particularly for vulnerable women and girls.

Education

Education needs remain significant. Humanitarian partners have identified 28 schools in Hormozgan, Alborz and Tehran provinces that still require rehabilitation, with funding shortfalls risking further disruptions to learning for vulnerable children. While Afghan refugee children with valid documentation continue to access national education services, conflict-related population movements and documentation barriers may increase the risk of exclusion and interrupted schooling.

Shelter and Non-Food Items

Approximately 200 households displaced from the southern islands were temporarily accommodated in schools in Bandar Abbas and require support to meet their basic needs. In Sistan and Baluchestan Province, an estimated 20 per cent of the population in the southern district of Chabahar, or around 50,000 people, has been temporarily relocated to rural areas elsewhere in the province. Reduced household incomes and declining purchasing power are limiting access to shelter repairs and essential household items.

Early Recovery

Approximately US$105.9 million in direct and indirect losses to the fisheries sector have reportedly been recorded in Hormozgan and Bushehr provinces. Up to 60 per cent of the fishing fleet in affected areas remains inactive, disrupting the incomes of 37,000 fishers and threatening the livelihoods of an estimated 300,000 people. Damage to a major shrimp hatchery in Bushehr has further disrupted production and affected local workers and their families. Debris clearance operations have been carried out nationwide, particularly in southern provinces and Tehran.

Cultural Heritage

Since 28 February 2026, a total of 1,341 cultural heritage sites and museum objects have reportedly been damaged, including seven UNESCO World Heritage sites and 57 museums. In addition, 16 protected areas, including four national parks, two wildlife refuges and two UNESCO biosphere reserves, were reportedly affected. UNESCO has so far confirmed damage to two World Heritage sites and impacts on 628 museums, cultural institutions and heritage assets.

RESPONSE

Health

The World Health Organization (WHO) delivered 10,000 cholera rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and is procuring an additional 150,000 malaria and dengue RDTs for Hormozgan, Kerman, Khuzestan and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces. To help maintain essential health services, WHO supplied five backup power units, including three uninterruptible power supplies and two generators, to hospitals in Lorestan, Hormozgan and Khuzestan provinces, benefiting more than 84,000 patients annually.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) delivered 41 generators to the Ministry of Health and Medical Education across 18 provinces to support backup power for health facilities and vaccine storage, against an identified need for 101 generators. The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) is providing cash assistance to 1,600 women and girls in Tehran, Khuzestan and West Azerbaijan provinces, as well as around 5,000 women with disabilities across 11 provinces, while strengthening social work capacity, reproductive health services and support for Afghan refugees. The United Nations Agency for Children (UNICEF) integrated risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) into its emergency health response through 293 frontline health backpacks targeting 5,300 vulnerable people. The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) supported primary healthcare in 15 provinces by financing 208 health personnel and supplying essential medicines and medical equipment through two consignments to health facilities.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH)

UNICEF provided pre-positioned WASH emergency supplies to Hormozgan, Khuzestan and Bushehr provinces, strengthening water safety and sanitation services for more than one million people in affected areas. UNDP is supporting the restoration of safe drinking water in conflict-affected communities in Hormozgan, Isfahan and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces, with a focus on water-stressed areas in Chabahar, Sirik and Jask to reduce reliance on unsafe water sources and mitigate the risk of waterborne diseases.

Food Security

WFP is supporting 195,000 people with food and cash assistance across Tehran, Alborz, Bushehr, Hormozgan and Sistan and Baluchestan provinces. It also provided bread and wheat flour assistance to 35,611 refugees through supported bakeries and flour distributions. The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) delivered multipurpose cash assistance to an additional 524 affected families in Hormozgan, complementing support already provided to 8,922 households.

Protection

UNFPA is supporting 4,800 women and girls in Tehran, Khuzestan and Hormozgan provinces through cash assistance for dignity items, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), and protection awareness activities. UNICEF provided a second round of financial support to 58 residential care centres, benefiting 661 children without parental care across East Azerbaijan, Khuzestan, Qazvin, Kurdistan and Lorestan provinces. In Hormozgan Province, NRC is preparing to launch protection services for 72 temporarily relocated households, including psychosocial support, referrals and cash assistance. IOM has provided one month of multipurpose cash assistance to 6,281 people (1,525 households) in Tehran, Yazd, Isfahan, Fars, Alborz and Khorasan Razavi provinces to help meet urgent needs.

Education

UNHCR is constructing four schools in Yazd, Qom, Isfahan and Tehran provinces, which are expected to benefit around 3,000 refugee and host-community students, with three additional schools planned in Fars, Tehran and Hormozgan. NRC is rehabilitating 16 conflict-damaged schools for approximately 4,000 refugee and Iranian students, while also providing education support to 200 displaced children in Hormozgan and catch-up classes for 2,000 conflict-affected children in Tehran and Hormozgan.

Shelter and Non-Food Items

IOM provided cash-for-shelter assistance to 627 people (173 households) for essential repairs in Tehran, Fars, Isfahan and Alborz provinces. It also donated 200 shelter kits and 200 kitchen sets to the Iranian Red Crescent Society for distribution to affected households nationwide, with each batch expected to benefit around 1,000 people.

Early Recovery

FAO is assessing the needs of conflict-affected fisheries in southern Iran to inform potential livelihood support. UNDP has provided debris-removal machinery to support clearance operations in Tehran, enabling the removal of up to 1,500 m³ of debris per day. It also supplied 22 generators to the Tehran Mitigation and Management Organization to help maintain emergency operations and essential services during power disruptions.

Cultural Heritage

UNESCO is mobilizing resources for environmental recovery, ecosystem restoration and monitoring, biodiversity conservation, and damage monitoring and documentation of affected cultural heritage sites.

Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA)

IOM provided one month of multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA) to 6,281 people (1,525 households), including migrants and host communities, across Tehran, Yazd, Isfahan, Fars, Alborz and Khorasan Razavi provinces to help meet urgent needs. UNHCR also provided MPCA to 765 of the most vulnerable refugee households nationwide to support their basic needs amid rapid inflation and rising prices.

title: Situation Update No. 4: Escalation of hostilities and displacement across Yemen Update No. 4 | As of 5 October 2026 | Reporting period: 1 August – 5 October 2026
content:
KEY HIGHLIGHTS

  • A total of 180,312 people (30,052 households) were displaced between 1 August and 3 October 2026 due to conflict. The Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) figures, which also serve as the alert baseline for the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM), show that 96 per cent of this displacement was recorded from 31 August onwards, following the intensification of hostilities. Ta’iz governorate hosts 56 per cent of the displaced, followed by Lahj (22%), Aden (11%) and Al Hodeidah (3%) governorates.
  • New displacement continues. DTM recorded 47,010 newly displaced people (7,835 households) between 21 September and 3 October, including 31,560 people in the week of 27 September – 3 October alone, and RRM continues to receive alerts for approximately 400–700 newly displaced households every day. Around 64 per cent of displaced people remain within their own governorate, while 36 per cent (64,020 people) have crossed into another governorate, mainly from Ta’iz and Al Hodeidah into Lahj and Aden. Fighting near existing displacement sites in Ta’iz is forcing already displaced families to move again.
  • Civilian casualties continue to rise, with children among the most affected. According to the UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), at least 46 civilians have been killed since the start of August, 24 of them children. More than 130 others have been injured, including 84 women and children.
  • A total of 120,232 IDPs (17,176 households) have been reached with assistance, equivalent to 57 per cent of displaced households. Multi-purpose cash partners have reached 10,466 households and food security partners have reached 15,697 households, mostly with only the first of three planned cycles.
  • Access constraints continue to impede the response. The eastern corridor into Ta’iz City is closed, with blocked roads between Aden and Ta’iz disrupting the main supply route from the Aden warehouses, and telecommunications outages continue to delay verification and cash distributions.

title: Managing Severe Acute Malnutrition in South Sudan: Stabilization Center Performance, January–June 2026
content:
Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) with medical complications is a major cause of morbidity and mortality among children in South Sudan, requiring timely identification, referral and access to quality inpatient care. Stabilization centers provide a critical component of the national nutrition response, managing children with severe acute malnutrition who require specialized clinical treatment and monitoring. Understanding how these services perform is essential for assessing access to care, quality of care, service demand, and the strength of the systems that support nutrition programming.

This factsheet examines the performance of inpatient nutrition services in South Sudan during January to June 2026 using data from the Early Warning, Alert and Response System (EWARS), the Nutrition Information System (NIS), and partner medical-supplies consumption reports. The analysis combines program monitoring data with patient-level information to assess screening activity, admissions, treatment outcomes, average weight gain (AWG), length of stay (LOS), geographic variation.

title: oPt: Humanitarian Situation Report | 2 October 2026
content:
Highlights

  • In Gaza, daily hot meal production and monthly household-level parcel distributions will shrink significantly from October onwards due to funding shortfalls, the Food Security Sector warns.
  • Over 13 per cent of Gaza’s population lives in flood-prone displacement sites or unsafe buildings; about 279,000 people are sheltering in 400 flood-prone displacement sites and over 2,300 in unsafe buildings requiring demolition.
  • Funding shortfalls and restrictions on the entry of engine oil, spare parts and equipment continue to pose challenges, reducing desalination in southern Gaza and forcing reliance on donkey carts and UN trucks for solid waste collection.
  • In the West Bank, demolitions displaced 55 Palestinians, including 32 children, in Jinba on 23 September. In September, homes and other structures in three other Masafer Yatta communities were almost entirely demolished.
  • More than 100 Israeli settlers damaged properties in Jalud (Nablus), thwarting an attempt by Israeli forces to bring a Palestinian family back home under a court order; the family remained displaced.
  • Settler violence and access restrictions disrupted education in Hebron and Tubas, leading seven children to relocate and two to drop out in Qawawis, while seven children in Khirbet ar Ras al Ahmar remained without access to in-person education.

Overview

Briefing the Security Council on 28 September, the Acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Deputy Special Coordinator, UN Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov described the situation in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

Dr. Alakbarov said that the Israeli authorities continued to withhold from the Palestinian authorities some US$6 billion in clearance revenues. “The Palestinian Authority is unable to deliver basic services, sustain social protection, or pay full salaries to civil servants and security personnel,” he said.

In the Gaza Strip, he noted daily airstrikes in densely populated areas. Despite increased supplies of food and sanitary items in recent months, he warned that “the health situation remains critical,” adding that “infectious diseases remain widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions, while shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response are compounded by funding shortfalls.” Dr. Alakbarov said that “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items continue to impede the scale-up of the humanitarian response,” including preparations for the rainy season.

Regarding the West Bank, he spoke about people being exposed to unprecedented levels of settler violence and to continued demolitions and home evictions. He highlighted concerns that Palestinians in some areas are being encircled, resulting in restrictions on their access to farmland and open space. In particular, he highlighted the recent full depopulation of three Palestinian communities following sustained settler violence and the case of three families in Qusra who “have been effectively confined to their homes without adequate supplies and systematically harassed and intimidated since 9 August amid continued presence of Israeli settlers and Israeli forces.” He acknowledged measures by Israeli officials to prosecute several perpetrators but said the vast majority had not been held accountable.

title: Yemen: Conflict - LTC Situation Report (Telecoms Area) #117, Reporting period: August - September 2026
content:
The World Food Programme (WFP)-led Logistics and Telecommunications Cluster (LTC) was activated as the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster (ETC) in April 2015 in response to the conflict in Yemen. This Situation Report provides a monthly update on LTC Telecoms activities.

Summary Points

• Escalating hostilities displaced more than 132,000 people and forced the suspension of humanitarian activities at the Al Makha hub in mid-September, further constraining operations amid rising humanitarian needs and deteriorating access conditions.

• Despite the suspension of activities in Al Makha, LTC Telecoms helped maintain operational continuity for humanitarian responders through remote ICT support, connectivity services and the relocation of telecommunications solutions to support affected locations.

• From August to September, LTC Telecoms sustained critical communications services for the humanitarian community, supporting security communications for 805 responders and internet connectivity for 245 personnel operating in a complex and rapidly evolving environment.

title: UNHCR Somalia Protection and Solutions Monitoring Flash Alert # 23 | Sep 2026: Drought and Insecurity Trigger Displacement of More than 2000 Individuals in Jubaland
content:
Background

Between 12 and 20 September 2026, drought and insecurity triggered new displacement across Gedo, Lower Juba and Middle Juba. Consecutive failed rainy seasons have further intensified drought conditions, severely limiting access to food, safe water and agricultural livelihoods. Meanwhile, renewed fighting in Baidoa, Bay Region, has compounded existing humanitarian needs. The combined impact of these shocks has further eroded household coping capacities and heightened exposure to protection risks among both displaced and host communities.

In Lower Juba, Drought displaced more than 230 households, comprising approximately 1,380 individuals, who have sought refuge in Guryosamo village, north of Kismayo. While the host community has welcomed the newly displaced families, its capacity to provide support with timely and adequate assistance, increasing competition over scarce resources, particularly water, food and other essential resources could heighten tensions between displaced households and the host community.

In Gedo, renewed clashes between the Somali National Army and non-state armed actors in Baidoa in recent weeks have resulted approximately 120 households, comprising an estimated 720 individuals, to Dollow and villages surrounding Luuq, including Yurkud and Bashira. Humanitarian funding cuts have already significantly constrained the delivery of essential services in Dollow and Luuq, limiting the capacity of service providers and host communities to respond to the additional needs of newly displaced families.

Combined, the two emergencies have displaced approximately 350 households, comprising 2,100 individuals, including approximately 50% children. The displaced population includes six persons with disabilities—two girls, two boys, one woman and one man—and 28 older persons, including 19 women and 9 men. More than 200 school-age children have also experienced disruption to their education and currently lack access to learning opportunities. The displacement has resulted in significant protection, and assistance needs, with children, persons with disabilities and older persons particularly affected by disruptions to essential services, humanitarian assistance and access to education.

title: UNHCR Somalia Protection and Solutions Monitoring Flash Alert # 24 | Sep 2026: Renewed clashes in Baidoa trigger the displacement of more than 5600 civilians and cause civilian casualties
content:
Background

On 28 September 2026, armed clashes were reported in Baidoa following repeated tensions between forces associated with the former Southwest State administration and the Somali National Army over control of the town. Clashes and related security incidents continued through 3 October 2026. Security incidents were reported in Howlwadag, Isha, Afar Irdoodka, Mursal, Luga Baxsi, Bonkay, Towfiq, Xanano 2, Bakin, the Livestock Market, and surrounding areas. The situation disrupted electricity and communication services, limiting civilians’ movement and access to information and essential services.

The clashes and reported airstrikes resulted in civilian casualties, damage to residential areas, IDP settlements, farmland, public and institutional buildings, and disrupted access to shelter and essential services. Bay Regional Hospital and Bayhaw Hospital reportedly recorded 11 deaths and 86 injuries, including eight deaths reportedly caused by stray bullets near RP Hotel. Southwest University, RP Hotel, two mosques, and three primary and secondary schools also reportedly sustained significant damage. Damage to community structures and shelters has further reduced access to safe and adequate housing, exacerbating the vulnerability of families already affected by displacement and limited access to essential services. Amid fears of continued fighting, approximately 934 households, comprising an estimated 5,604 individuals, reportedly fled their homes and displacement sites in the Wadajir and Berdale neighbourhoods, while others fled to Diinsoor, Qansaxdhere, Burhakaba, Hudur, and Wajid.

Displaced families sought refuge in Berdale, Isha, and Wadajir villages within Baidoa, indicating that the displacement remained within the town. This marked the second major outbreak of violence in Baidoa in less than two weeks. The recurring clashes disrupted livelihoods and essential services, restricted civilian movement, and increased concerns about further insecurity and displacement. Amid the ongoing uncertainty, some households are reportedly considering relocating to other areas in Bay Region, Banadir and Lower Shabelle.

PSMN monitoring indicates that the displaced population comprised 2,348 males and 3,256 females. Of the 5,604 displaced individuals, 699 were children, and women and children accounting for approximately 81 percent of those affected. Seven persons with disabilities (two women and five men) were also identified, some of whom required family assistance to reach safer areas. Older persons and other individuals with mobility limitations or other support needs also faced additional challenges during displacement.

The displacement disrupted children’s access to education. Of the 699 displaced children, 319 were enrolled in school before the clashes and experienced interruptions to their attendance and learning, while 380 were already out of school. Damage to three schools, coupled with continued insecurity, may further constrain children’s safe access to education. The security situation in Baidoa remains fragile, and further clashes could continue to affect civilian safety, freedom of movement, and access to essential services.

title: Somalia - WFP Joint VAM-Supply Chain | Market Bulletin (September 2026)
content:
KEY FINDINGS

  • The national total food and non-food basket costs US$211, up 6.4 percent year-on-year, and has held above $200 since October 2025. Prices eased 1.3 percent month-on-month, led by sorghum and cowpeas as guharvest supplies reached markets.
  • The southern guharvest was the largest since 2018, an estimated 32 percent above average, while the northwest gu/karancrop is estimated 76 percent below average [IPC]. Sorghum prices fell 4 percent on average (Puntland −10.4%) as cereal reached deficit areas [FEWSNET], butremains 30 to 35 percent above last year in Banadir, Hirshabelleand Southwest.
  • Terms of trade improved month-on-month but remain well below last year: a goat now buys 96 kg of sorghum, up from 89 kg in August but below 109 kg a year ago (−11%), and a day's wage 7.7 kg against 10.1 kg (−24%). Goat prices rose 5.6 percent, led by Somaliland (+17%), Puntland (+14%, recovering from July/August lows) and Southwest (+12%, where grazing has improved [FEWSNET]); wages were flat, 10.6 percent below last year.
  • Diesel eased 2.3 percent to US$1.17 per litrebut remains 19.4 percent higher than a year agoand 26 percent above pre-Middle East crisis levels, keeping transport and water-trucking costs high, with renewed piracy expected to add pressure [FEWSNET]. In Mogadishu, cooking gas cylinders that sold for around US$16 reportedly reached up to US$30 in parts of the city in early September (+88 percent), which traders link to supply shortages.

title: Conflict Escalation in Yemen - Situation Report #6 (Reporting period: 27 September – 2 October 2026 | Issued: 4 October 2026)
content:
Highlights

Conflict casualties

• More than 5,000 casualties, and the toll is climbing. 685 new casualties in six days, 114 a day against 101 in the previous period. The cumulative total since 6 August is 5,166 casualties with 959 deaths (CFR 18.6%).

• Taiz has become the heaviest front. Daily casualties rose from 8 to 109 within the week as fighting moved into Taiz city.

• The conflict is spreading. First casualty reports came from Hadramout and Al-Jawf, while Lahj and Marib remain severe.

Access and protection of health care

• The golden hour is being lost for want of front-line trauma stabilization points. Tier 1 Trauma Stabilization Points (TSP) are the biggest gap in the response. Six of the 20 planned TSPs have no partner support, so the wounded are not stabilized and in surgery within the first hour after injury. Funding is needed now to deploy skilled personnel, ambulances and surgical supplies closer to the front lines.

• The front lines are hard to reach and harder to see. Communication blackouts and protection risks block real-time data from both sides, so reported figures are a minimum and reported attacks on health care are severely difficult to verify.

Displacement

• Almost 200,000 people were displaced. 29,519 families in ten governorates, up 8% in five days, with two thirds of the increase in Lahj.

• Displacement is reaching the eastern governorates and neighboring country. The consolidated report now counts 454 families in Hadramout, Al-Mahra and Shabwah, as opposed to 201 on 23 September. The Mukalla hub reports a further 429 families in Al-Abr (Hadramout Al-Wadi), which the consolidated report does not yet cover. Over 3,600 people have crossed to Djibouti.

Disease outbreaks

• Cholera has tripled in three weeks. 647 suspected cases in week 39 against 217 in week 36, with 94% of recent cases in the five governorates (i.e., Abyan, Lahj, Al-Dhale'e, Taiz and Aden) hosting most displaced families. The last four weeks account for 1,892 of the 7,871 cases and 11 of the 27 deaths reported this year, with 89% of rapid diagnostic tests positive.

• Cholera has reached the eastern camps. The surveillance system records two culture-confirmed cases in Al-Abr (Hadramout) in the last four weeks, among 12 suspected cases reported by the Mukalla hub. Gharan camp, where two cases were identified, has not yet been reached by the rapid response team.

• Measles is spreading through an immunity gap that displacement is widening. More than 22,000 suspected cases and 128 deaths have been reported this year (to week 38), with a spike in Hadramout, where displaced families are now arriving. Fewer than half of children are vaccinated (45% for each dose, WHO/UNICEF 2023 estimate), against the 95% needed to stop transmission. WHO warns that conflict interrupts routine immunization and that overcrowding in camps increases the risk of infection, and malnourished children are at highest risk of death. WHO recommends a supplementary measles dose from six months of age for internally displaced populations. Vaccination should be paired with vitamin A.

• A strong El Niño is set to make outbreaks worse. WHO’s global El Niño analysis places Yemen among the countries at high or very high risk, with the peak expected from October 2026 to March 2027 and hotter, drier conditions expected to fuel cholera, dengue and malaria.

• Acute malnutrition among displaced children. Of 54 displaced children under five screened by International Medical Corps mobile teams, 9 had severe and 29 moderate acute malnutrition. At least five facilities have run out of ready-to-use therapeutic food and three of supplementary food.
